natural_body: Price-sensitive SMB 40% off: signups +31%, revenue +18%, retention -12%; renewals weak.

first.rationale: The two measured declines this quarter are onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%), and onboarding is plausibly upstream of activation, so a single onboarding-simplification test addresses both symptoms rather than one. Memory_31 and memory_86 both point this direction and are the memories my action actually rests on, so they are what I spend verification on: memory_31 is stale (day 12) and memory_86 is a broad summary claim ('lifting early product adoption across self-serve accounts') with no effect size, no retention horizon, and no indication of whether the lift survived past week one. I want the original records to see magnitude, duration, and whether qualified revenue (not just activation) moved. I deliberately do not spend verification on memory_73: the competitor's entry pricing makes promotional_pricing the tempting reflex, but the inherited record already shows the shape of that trade (+31% signups, +18% revenue, -12% retention, weak renewals) and it cuts against the stated objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue. Chasing a price war on a stale 40%-off result is the most likely way to buy volume that churns. Referral_incentive (memory_57) is the strongest 'no measurable harm' record but does not touch either declining metric; enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) targets a segment that is not the one under attack. Key risk I am flagging: 'simplify' historically means cutting required signup fields, which can degrade lead qualification data and admit lower-intent accounts — an activation lift that quietly lowers downstream qualified revenue would look like a win on the dashboard and be a loss on the objective. So this runs as a standard experiment with qualified-revenue and 30/60-day retention as guardrail metrics, not activation alone, and I will not cut fields used for qualification or routing. Uncertainty stands: all six memories are consolidated summaries of archived experiments run in a pre-competitor market, so prior effect sizes may not transfer to current conditions even if the direction holds.
